title: Sensex's 10.6% Seven-Session Pre-Diwali Rally Is Its Strongest in 35 Years
headline: Sensex's 10.6% Seven-Session Pre-Diwali Rally Is Its Strongest in 35 Years
subheadline: The Sensex closed at 81,028 and the Nifty reclaimed 25,000 on Friday as foreign investors poured in about Rs 49,500 crore, crude slid and the market posted its best week since February 2021.
summary: The Sensex closed at 81,028 and the Nifty reclaimed 25,000 on Friday as foreign investors poured in about Rs 49,500 crore, crude slid and the market posted its best week since February 2021.
excerpt: The Sensex closed at 81,028 and the Nifty reclaimed 25,000 on Friday as foreign investors poured in about Rs 49,500 crore, crude slid and the market posted its best week since February 2021.
body:
• The Sensex has risen 10.6% — 7,782 points — across seven straight winning sessions into Diwali, its strongest seven-session pre-Diwali run in 35 years, since 1991.
  • On Friday the Sensex closed up 1,718 points (2.17%) at 81,028.02 and the Nifty gained 494 points (2.01%) to 25,030.35, both reclaiming psychologically watched levels for the first time in more than nine months.
  • Foreign portfolio investors bought about Rs 49,500 crore (roughly $5.2 billion) of Indian stocks on a net basis during the run, per NSDL and BSE data reported by The Times of India.
  • The week itself — Sensex up 8.8% — was the market's best since February 2021, and it added about Rs 29.57 lakh crore to investor wealth. Next up is the Muhurat trading session on Diwali day, Sunday, November 8.

Indian equities go into Diwali on a run for the record books. The BSE Sensex closed Friday at 81,028.02, up 1,718 points or 2.17% on the day, completing seven consecutive winning sessions that have lifted the index 7,782 points, or 10.6% — its strongest seven-session advance before Diwali in 35 years, since 1991, and its best seven-day percentage gain since February 2021, according to Dow Jones market data reported by Morningstar. The Nifty 50 rose 494 points (2.01%) on Friday to 25,030.35, up 10.27% across the seven sessions.

Both benchmarks are back above levels last seen more than nine months ago — the Sensex over 80,000 and the Nifty over 25,000 — and the week's 8.8% Sensex gain is the biggest weekly rise since the vaccine-driven rally week of February 2021. The combined market capitalisation of BSE-listed companies rose about Rs 29.57 lakh crore from October 28 to Rs 503.11 lakh crore.

What drove it

The proximate cause was foreign money coming back. Foreign portfolio investors bought Indian stocks worth about Rs 49,500 crore — roughly $5.2 billion — on a net basis during the rally, The Times of India reported, citing NSDL and BSE data. Behind the flows: crude oil prices fell about 20% in under two weeks, the US midterm results raised hopes of policy stability and of a diplomatic easing in West Asia, and Indian companies delivered a solid set of quarterly earnings, with new listings such as Jio Platforms adding momentum, according to Upstox's market wrap. Mahindra & Mahindra, Shriram Finance, Bajaj Finance, Reliance Industries, Jio Financial and HDFC Bank were among the leading gainers.

Friday's session made the point about the rally's domestic engine: Indian indices rose more than 2% even as US markets and AI stocks sold off sharply overnight — the same global rout that, earlier in the autumn, dragged Indian IT stocks around. Our earlier report on the first leg of the post-midterm surge traces how the move began.

The case for caution

A 10.6% rise in seven sessions prices in a great deal of good news quickly. The Sensex is still about 5.6% below its record close of 85,836.12 from September 2024, and market commentators flag profit-booking risk with the Nifty now testing the 25,000 zone it has just reclaimed. The calendar offers an immediate sentiment check: the special Muhurat trading session on Diwali day, Sunday, November 8, which opens the new Samvat year, followed by the regular week in which investors will see whether foreign buying survives at these levels.

For diaspora investors watching from North America, the practical read is narrow: the rally is flow-driven and broad, led by financials and large caps, and its durability now depends on FPI follow-through rather than on any single earnings print.
